terms.gloss: a faun, a woodland spirit: for an elf
terms.comment: Classically the Fauni, in the plural, are the woodland spirits of the Italian countryside, goat-footed like Pan, whom country people believed they heard at night in lonely places, playing and making music (Lucretius). Fairy-tale elves have no ancient counterpart; this is the nearest classical being, and its use for an elf is ours. For a female one, nympha (see “nymph” and “fairy”).

terms.gloss: a goblin who sits on buried treasure
evidence: Petr. 38: quom Incubōnī pilleum rapuisset, et thēsaurum invēnit
terms.comment: In the talk of Trimalchio’s freedmen, the spirit that guards buried treasure: snatch his cap and you find the treasure. Lewis & Short marks the word post-classical; a goblin rather than an elf.

phrases.latin: Noctū faunī in silvā lūdunt et cantant.
phrases.english: At night the elves play and sing in the wood.

phrases.latin: haec loca capripedēs Satyrōs Nymphāsque tenēre fīnitimī fingunt et Faunōs esse locuntur
phrases.english: the people round about imagine that goat-footed satyrs and nymphs live in these places, and they say there are fauns

phrases.latin: quom Incubōnī pilleum rapuisset, et thēsaurum invēnit
phrases.english: when he snatched a goblin’s cap, he found a treasure too

sources: Lewis & Short: Faunus · Lewis & Short: incubo
